messages.subject: How can I abort a chain (and maybe rerun)?

It would be even better if that chain can be restarted with a different initialization.

Thanks,
Jingjing

Ah, that was Andrew being facetious.  “Sampling Through Adaptive Neighborhoods”
is his favorite backronym for “Stan”.
On Aug 14, 2016, at 10:15 PM, Chen Jingjing <chen...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thanks for your thorough explanation! Actually that is my impression when I read your previous response. However when I read Andrew's comment, "kinda sampling through neighborhoods that are, y'know, adaptive", I thought it meant that the chains interact with each other, otherwise what does "adaptive" mean here? Please correct me if I am wrong. I only have very basic understanding of Hamiltonian MC and Stan.

Thanks,
Jingjing

2016-08-14 23:30 GMT-04:00 Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com>:
You are misunderstanding the problem here.  The chains do not interact
and hence do not affect each other.  Rather the fundamental issue is that
a Markov transition will yield a good Markov chain with respect to a given
target distribution only when _all chains achieve the same behavior
independently of each other_.  If any chain behaves differently than the
others then there is some pathological neighborhood of parameter space
that the other chains just haven’t encountered yet.


On Aug 14, 2016, at 9:46 AM, Chen Jingjing <chen...@gmail.com> wrote:

I actually don't know that chains will affect each other in Stan. And I am not sure how it works. Is the actual algorithm explained in Stan reference book or something else?

As for the problem I am having now, shall I simply run one chain at a time so that a bad chain would not affect the others, and then repeatedly run a few dozens of chains and select the best one?

Thanks,
Jingjing 

2016-08-12 16:21 GMT-04:00 Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu>:
Stan is, umm, kinda sampling through neighborhoods that are, y'know, adaptive.

On Aug 12, 2016, at 1:36 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

Because MCMC works only when all chains are exploring the same neighborhoods.  If any are exceptional chains then there are subtle pathologies in the interaction of the Markov transition and target distribution that affect the Markov transition itself and hence all of the chains.  This is why running multiple chains is so useful.

On Aug 12, 2016, at 10:31, Jingjing Chen <chen...@gmail.com> wrote:

Why should I suspect the other chains when one of them is misbehaving? I thought that the chains don't affect each other in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Is that true?

在 2016年8月12日星期五 UTC-4下午1:23:18，Michael Betancourt写道：
Never ever ever do this.  If even one chain is misbehaving then it indicates that all of the chains are biased and should be suspect.  I'd also be surprised if all of our other diagnostics are not going crazy.

Dear Stan Users,

I finished running a chain and found that its so stuck in the same place that some of the parameters literally never change during the second half of the chain (and the first half is thrown away and not recorded),  with a standard deviation of 10^-13. It happened once with my model. Other chains seems fine. I am wondering if there is a way I can diagnose the useless chains and abort them. It would be even better if that chain can be restarted with a different initialization.

Thanks,
Jingjing

Hi, yes I meant "adaptive," but the way that this is currently implemented in Stan is separately for each chain. It would be possible to have adaptation that would use chains together--such algorithms exist--but this is not how we are doing things in Stan right now.

Thanks for your thorough explanation! Actually that is my impression when I read your previous response. However when I read Andrew's comment, "kinda sampling through neighborhoods that are, y'know, adaptive", I thought it meant that the chains interact with each other, otherwise what does "adaptive" mean here? Please correct me if I am wrong. I only have very basic understanding of Hamiltonian MC and Stan.

Thanks,
Jingjing

2016-08-14 23:30 GMT-04:00 Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com>:
You are misunderstanding the problem here.  The chains do not interact
and hence do not affect each other.  Rather the fundamental issue is that
a Markov transition will yield a good Markov chain with respect to a given
target distribution only when _all chains achieve the same behavior
independently of each other_.  If any chain behaves differently than the
others then there is some pathological neighborhood of parameter space
that the other chains just haven’t encountered yet.

As for the problem I am having now, shall I simply run one chain at a time so that a bad chain would not affect the others, and then repeatedly run a few dozens of chains and select the best one?

Thanks,
Jingjing 

2016-08-12 16:21 GMT-04:00 Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu>:
Stan is, umm, kinda sampling through neighborhoods that are, y'know, adaptive.

On Aug 12, 2016, at 1:36 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

Because MCMC works only when all chains are exploring the same neighborhoods.  If any are exceptional chains then there are subtle pathologies in the interaction of the Markov transition and target distribution that affect the Markov transition itself and hence all of the chains.  This is why running multiple chains is so useful.

On Aug 12, 2016, at 10:31, Jingjing Chen <chen...@gmail.com> wrote:

Why should I suspect the other chains when one of them is misbehaving? I thought that the chains don't affect each other in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Is that true?

在 2016年8月12日星期五 UTC-4下午1:23:18，Michael Betancourt写道：
Never ever ever do this.  If even one chain is misbehaving then it indicates that all of the chains are biased and should be suspect.  I'd also be surprised if all of our other diagnostics are not going crazy.

parts:
Andrew was just making a joke. See:

http://andrewgelman.com/2016/03/15/stan-backronym-just-a-joke/

If you want to understand how Stan adapts during warmup,
it's explained in the manual. We have to adapt the mass matrix
(basically scale of each parameter by default) and step size (HMC
uses an iterative algorithm for integrating the Hamiltonian)
for HMC, but it's done independently in each chain.

The chains *do not* communicate with each other during warmup.
As Andrew said (joking aside), they could, but they don't in
the current (2.11) version of Stan.

- Bob
